label: Separated property, rational and conceptual moral-supervenience claims from primary evidence
summary: Read materialized Railton 1986 (p.165), Boyd's How to be a Moral Realist (§5.3 pp.345–349) and the exact pinned SEP §3.4. Railton endorses property-level natural supervenience but says reduction 'may' obtain and does not specify weak/strong/global scope. Boyd's much more specific rational supervenience concerns approximate actual-case judgments under prevailing standards and conditional mutual ratification of plausible theories' epistemic-contact/error accounts; he acknowledges apparent failures and offers fallibility/non-bivalence diagnoses. Blackburn's reported challenge instead asks why competent predication must respect supervenience analytically even if there is no analytic natural-to-moral entailment. The strongest live cognitivist replies contest his no-entailment or belief/motivation assumptions, not his positive purposes explanation. Rejected identifying Boyd's rational supervenience with `Competence` or `Strong`, inferring metaphysical necessitation from observed rational agreement, and treating Railton's 'may be reducible' as accomplished reduction. The source-backed comparison, provisional assessment and exact unresolved bridges live in docs/naturalistic-moral-realism.md (moral-supervenience section). No fresh Lean theorem, historical worldview model, root premise closure or philosophical rival defeat is claimed.
blocker: OPEN: Boyd's actual-case, plausible-theory and bivalence diagnoses need independent counterexample-sensitive support. Railton's complete natural property base and reduction/identification are not established. Blackburn's conceptual competence explanation needs comparison against an adequate cognitivist semantics of analyticity and motivation; source treatment of Blackburn is secondhand pending his 1993 primary pages. None of these bridges licenses equating epistemic, analytic and modal necessity. A new Lean theorem would require an interpretation and a working pinned Lean/Comparator environment, unavailable locally in this worktree; retain these precise source propositions without a simulated formal result.
